blocks.t: Collision theory explains how reactions occur. Reactant particles must form a homogeneous mixture and collide with one another.

blocks.label: Activation Energy
blocks.text: The minimum amount of energy, required for an effective collision between the reacting species, is called activation energy.

blocks.t: Most reactions are slow because most collisions are ineffective — particles lack sufficient energy OR are not properly oriented.

items.q: What role does the activation energy play in chemical reactions?
items.ans: Role of Activation Energy: Ea acts as an energy barrier. Only particles with energy ≥ Ea can undergo effective collision and form products. A lower Ea means more particles can react → faster rate.

items.q: How does the activation energy affect the rate of a reaction?
items.ans:
Lower Ea → more particles have sufficient energy → more effective collisions → faster rate.
Higher Ea → fewer particles can react → slower rate.
This is why a catalyst (which lowers Ea) speeds up a reaction.

blocks.label: Rate of Reaction
blocks.text: The rate of a reaction is defined as the change in the concentration of a reactant or a product divided by the time taken for the change.

blocks.t:
Rate of reaction = ΔC / Δt

For:  A → B
Rate = –Δ[A]/Δt  =  +Δ[B]/Δt

Units:
  Fast reaction  →  mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
  Slow reaction  →  mol dm⁻³ min⁻¹  or  mol dm⁻³ h⁻¹
  Gas phase      →  pressure units used instead of mol dm⁻³

blocks.head: Sign Convention
blocks.body: The sign in the rate expression tells us whether a species is being consumed or formed:
items: Negative sign (–Δ[A]/Δt): reactant A is being consumed → concentration decreasing.
Positive sign (+Δ[B]/Δt): product B is being formed → concentration increasing.

rows: Rate at any one instant during the reaction
dC/dt — slope of tangent to curve at that point
Rate over a time period between two specific intervals
ΔC/Δt — change in concentration ÷ time interval

blocks.t: Initially, instantaneous rate > average rate. At the end of the interval, instantaneous rate < average rate. They are equal for only one instant in any time interval.

blocks.head: Sample Problem 7.1 — Haber Process
blocks.body: N₂(aq) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g). [NH₃] = 3.5 mol dm⁻³ at 1.0 min; [NH₃] = 6.2 mol dm⁻³ at 4.0 min.
blocks.eq:
i) Instantaneous rate at 1.0 min:
   Rate = ΔC/Δt = 3.5 / 1.0 = 3.5 mol dm⁻³ min⁻¹

ii) Average rate from 1.0 to 4.0 min:
   ΔC = 6.2 – 3.5 = 2.7 mol dm⁻³
   Δt = 4.0 – 1.0 = 3.0 min
   Rate = 2.7 / 3.0 = 0.90 mol dm⁻³ min⁻¹

items.q: H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2HI(g). At 100.0 s, iodine concentration fell from 0.010 to 0.0080 mol dm⁻³. What is the average rate?

blocks.t: 7.2.2 Measuring the Rate of a Chemical Reaction
To find rate graphically: plot concentration (y-axis) vs time (x-axis). Draw a tangent at the desired time point. The slope of the tangent = instantaneous rate at that point.

blocks.head: Reading Rate from a Graph — HI Decomposition Example
blocks.body: 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g) at 508°C. See Table 7.1 and Figure 7.2 in book.
blocks.eq:
At 100 s, tangent gives:
  ΔC = 0.04 mol dm⁻³ over 100 s

Rate = ΔC/Δt = 0.04 / 100 = 4×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
blocks.note: If a product (H₂ or I₂) is plotted instead, a rising curve is obtained. The tangent at 100 s gives the same rate value.

blocks.caption: Concentration–time graph for 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g) at 508°C. Tangent drawn at 100 s gives rate = 4×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
blocks.alt: Falling hyperbolic curve with tangent drawn at t=100 s. Triangle ABC shows ΔC=0.04 mol dm⁻³ over Δt=100 s.

blocks.head: Why Rate Decreases with Time
items: Reactants are consumed → concentration falls.
Fewer particles per unit volume → fewer collisions.
Rate of forward reaction decreases.
Graph slope becomes less steep with time → slope = 0 at completion.

items.q: What do you deduce about the rate of the reaction with time from these calculations?
items.ans: Rate decreases with time. As [HI] falls, fewer HI molecules collide effectively per second → lower rate. The concentration–time graph slope becomes less steep as time passes.

items.q: At which concentration is the rate highest, and lowest?
items.ans:
Highest rate at highest [HI] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³ (start of reaction).
Lowest rate at lowest [HI] = 0.02 mol dm⁻³ (near completion).

items.title: Chemical Method (Titration)
items.body: — Most suitable for reactions in solution (e.g. esterification, hydrolysis of esters). Steps: (1) Allow reactants under specific conditions. (2) Remove small sample at set time interval. (3) Cool in ice-cold water to stop reaction (quench). (4) Titrate against NaOH with phenolphthalein indicator → gives acid concentration. Repeat at various intervals.

items.title: Spectrophotometry / Colorimetry
items.body: — Used if reactant or product absorbs UV, visible, or IR radiation. Rate ∝ amount of radiation absorbed. As reactant is used up, absorption changes → rate can be tracked. E.g. alcohol → aldehyde → alcohol (colorimetric change).

items.title: Electrical Conductivity Method
items.body: — Used for reactions involving ions. Rate ∝ conductivity (when ions are formed). Rate ∝ 1/conductivity (when ions are combined). E.g. neutralisation, solubility of ionic compounds.

items.title: Volume Change Method (Volumetric Method)
items.body: — Used for gas-phase reactions where volume/pressure changes. Rate ∝ volume change (ΔV) or pressure change. E.g. CO + H₂ → CH₃OH (methanol synthesis). Rate observed by measuring gas volume change or pressure change over time.

sections.title: Factors Affecting Rate of a Chemical Reaction

items: Concentration of the reactants
Temperature of the system
Surface area
Catalyst

blocks.head: Effect of Concentration on Rate
blocks.body: According to the law of mass action: greater the concentration of reactants → more rapidly the reaction proceeds.
items: More concentration → more particles per unit volume → more chances of collision.
More effective collisions → higher rate.
Less concentration → fewer collisions → lower rate.
For gaseous reactions: increasing pressure increases gas concentration → rate increases (no effect on solids/liquids).
Example: When CO₂ concentration is high, rate of photosynthesis is higher.

blocks.t: Increasing temperature increases rate. Rate either doubles or triples for every 10°C rise in temperature. Rate ∝ frequency of collisions ∝ energy ∝ Temperature.

blocks.label: Boltzmann Distribution Curve
blocks.text: The Boltzmann distribution curve is a graph that shows the distribution of energies at certain temperature.

blocks.head: Maxwell-Boltzmann Curve — Key Points
blocks.body: Graph: number of molecules (y-axis) vs kinetic/molecular energy (x-axis) at a given temperature.
items: Few molecules have very low energy.
Few molecules have very high energy.
Most molecules have moderate (average) energy.
Area under curve = total number of molecules.
Shaded area (E ≥ Ea) = molecules with enough energy for effective collision.
Number of molecules with effective collision ∝ shaded area.

blocks.caption: Boltzmann distribution curve at one temperature T showing Ea marked by vertical line and shaded area representing molecules with E ≥ Ea.
blocks.alt: Bell-shaped asymmetric curve peaking then trailing off. Vertical line at Ea on x-axis. Area to the right of Ea is shaded.

blocks.head: Effect of Temperature Rise on Boltzmann Curve
blocks.body: When temperature increases from T₁ to T₂ (T₂ > T₁):
items: Curve flattens (peak lowers) and shifts to the right.
Shaded area increases — more molecules have E ≥ Ea.
More molecules undergo effective collisions → rate increases.
For 10°C rise: shaded area approximately doubles → rate doubles or triples.

blocks.caption: Boltzmann distribution at T₁ and T₂ (T₂ > T₁). T₂ curve is flatter/wider with a larger shaded area to right of Ea.
blocks.alt: Two overlapping bell curves. T₁ is taller and narrower. T₂ is flatter and wider with peak shifted right. Shaded areas to right of Ea shown; T₂ shaded area is larger.

items.q: What is the Boltzmann distribution curve?
items.ans: It is a graph between number of molecules (y-axis) and their molecular energy (x-axis). It shows the distribution of kinetic energies at a specific temperature. At any temperature: few have very low energy, few have very high energy, and most have moderate energy. The shaded area (E ≥ Ea) shows molecules capable of effective collision.

items.q: Explain why a 10°C rise in temperature approximately doubles the rate of a reaction.
items.ans: When temperature rises by 10°C, molecules gain more kinetic energy. The Boltzmann curve flattens and shifts to the right. The shaded area (E ≥ Ea) approximately doubles. This means twice as many molecules can undergo effective collisions per second → rate doubles (or triples).

blocks.head: Effect of Surface Area
blocks.body: Rate ∝ surface area ∝ number of binding/active sites exposed.
items: Greater surface area = more particles exposed = more chances of collision.
Powdered solids react faster than lumps of the same solid.
Example: Wood burns more rapidly when chopped into small pieces.

blocks.label: Catalyst
blocks.text: A catalyst is defined as a substance which alters the rate of a chemical reaction, but remains chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction.

blocks.label: Catalysis
blocks.text: The process, which takes place in the presence of a catalyst, is called catalysis.

blocks.head: How a Catalyst Works
blocks.body: A catalyst provides a new reaction path with a lower activation energy barrier.
items: Catalyst brings molecules into correct orientation.
Provides alternative pathway with lower Ea.
More molecules now have energy ≥ new (lower) Ea → more effective collisions → rate increases.
Without catalyst: reaction occurs at slower speed.
Catalyst is NOT consumed — regenerated at end of reaction.
Common catalysts: Pt, Ni, H₂SO₄.

blocks.caption: Energy profile diagram for uncatalyzed (high peak) and catalyzed (low peak) reaction. Reactants and products at the same energy level in both cases.
blocks.alt: Two energy curves from Reactants to Products. Uncatalyzed: tall peak (large Ea without catalyst). Catalyzed: shorter peak (smaller Ea with catalyst). Products energy is the same for both.

rxns.note: Catalyst: H⁺ (H₂SO₄); acid hydrolysis of ester

rows: Catalyst and reactants are in the SAME phase
Catalyst and reactants are in DIFFERENT phases
Usually solid; reactants are gas or liquid

blocks.head: Enzymes — Nature's Catalysts
blocks.body: Biochemical catalysts (enzymes) lower Ea in living organisms. Enzymes are typically proteins. Factors affecting enzyme activity: pH, temperature, substrate concentration.
items: Vitamins can act as coenzymes — help enzymes catalyze reactions more efficiently.
Vitamin K: necessary for blood clotting.

items.q: Can a catalyst be consumed in a chemical reaction? Why or why not?
items.ans: No. By definition, a catalyst remains chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction. It provides an alternative lower-energy pathway and is regenerated at the end.

items.q: Is 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g) with V₂O₅(solid) homogeneous or heterogeneous catalysis?
items.ans: Heterogeneous catalysis. V₂O₅ is a solid while the reactants SO₂ and O₂ are gases — they are in different phases.

sections.title: Rate Law, Rate Constant and Order of Reaction

blocks.label: Rate Law
blocks.text: The representation of rate of a reaction in terms of concentration of the reactants is known as rate law.

blocks.head: Rate Law Equation
blocks.body: For reaction:  aA + bB → cC + dD
blocks.eq:
Rate = k [A]ˣ [B]ʸ

  k  = rate constant (proportionality constant)
  x  = order w.r.t. A  (from experiment)
  y  = order w.r.t. B  (from experiment)
  x+y = overall order of reaction
blocks.note: x and y are experimentally determined. They may or may NOT equal the stoichiometric coefficients a and b in the balanced equation.

blocks.label: Rate Constant (k)
blocks.text: The specific rate constant of a chemical reaction is the rate of reaction when the concentrations of the reactants are unity.

blocks.t: Rate constant (from notes): Ratio between rate of reaction and molar concentration of reactants. When [A] = [B] = 1 mol dm⁻³, Rate = k. k is constant at a given temperature but changes with temperature.

blocks.label: Order of Reaction
blocks.text: The order of a reaction with respect to a specific reactant is the exponent applied to that reactant's concentration within the rate equation.

blocks.head: Key Facts About Reaction Order
blocks.body: Order of reaction (n) = sum of exponents of molar concentrations in the rate equation.
items: Always determined experimentally — NEVER from the balanced equation.
Value may be zero, whole number, or a fraction.
For single-step reactions, molecularity and reaction order are the same.
For multi-step reactions, order is determined from the slow (rate-determining) step.
Example: 2H₂ + 2NO → N₂ + H₂O; rate = k[H₂][NO]²; order w.r.t. H₂ = 1; w.r.t. NO = 2; overall = 3.

blocks.t: The order of reaction CANNOT be deduced from the balanced equation. Exponents x and y in Rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ must come from experimental data (kinetic measurements).

items.q: How is the order of reaction derived from the rate law?
items.ans: The order w.r.t. each reactant is the exponent (power) of that reactant's concentration in the rate law equation. These exponents are found experimentally. The overall order = sum of all exponents. Example: Rate = k[A]²[B]¹ → overall order = 2+1 = 3.

items.q: Explain the specific rate constant of a reaction and how it is represented.
items.ans: The specific rate constant (k) equals the rate of reaction when all reactant concentrations are unity (1 mol dm⁻³). In Rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ, when [A]=[B]=1: Rate = k×1×1 = k. It is constant at a given temperature but changes with temperature.

blocks.head: Zero Order Reaction
blocks.body: The rate of a zero order reaction is independent of the concentration of the reactants. A change in concentration has no effect on the speed of the reaction.
blocks.eq:
A → Product
Rate = k[A]⁰ = k

Unit of k = mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
items: Photochemical reactions are usually zero order.
H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g) [sunlight]; Rate = k[H₂]⁰[Cl₂]⁰ = k
2NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) [high T, catalyst]; Rate = k[NH₃]⁰ = k
Photosynthesis is also zero order.

blocks.head: First Order Reaction
blocks.body: A reaction for which the sum of the exponents of concentrations in the rate equation is 1. Rate depends on initial concentration of ONE reactant.
blocks.eq:
Rate = k[A]¹

Unit of k = s⁻¹
items: One reactant may be in excess (i) or absent in the slow step (ii).
Example: N₂O₅(g) → 2NO₂(g) + ½O₂(g); Rate = k[N₂O₅]¹
Example: R–Cl + H₂O → R–OH + HX; Rate = k[R–X]¹; H₂O is in excess
Nuclear (radioactive) decay is ALWAYS first order.

blocks.head: Second Order Reaction
blocks.body: A reaction for which sum of exponents of concentrations in the rate equation is 2.
blocks.eq:
Rate = k[A]²         (one reactant, order = 2)
Rate = k[A]¹[B]¹     (two reactants, 1+1 = 2)

Unit of k = dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
items: Two reactants may be similar or different.
Example: C₂H₅Cl + CN⁻ → C₂H₅CN + Cl⁻; Rate = k[C₂H₅Cl][CN⁻]; order = 1+1 = 2
Example: NO + O₃ → NO₂ + O₂; Rate = k[NO][O₃]; order = 1+1 = 2

blocks.head: Third Order Reaction
blocks.body: A reaction for which sum of exponents of concentrations in the rate equation is 3.
blocks.eq:
Rate = k[A]³                  (n = 3)
Rate = k[A]²[B]¹              (n = 2+1 = 3)
Rate = k[A]¹[B]¹[C]¹          (n = 1+1+1 = 3)

Unit of k = dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹
items: Example: 2FeCl₃ + 6KI → 2FeI₂ + 6KCl + I₂; Rate = k[FeCl₃][KI]²; order = 1+2 = 3
Example: 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g); Rate = k[NO]²[O₂]¹; order = 2+1 = 3

blocks.head: BOOK ERROR — Page 152
blocks.wrong: Book writes '2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g), Rate = k[NO]²[O₂]¹, order = 1+1 = 2' under the Third Order Reaction examples.
blocks.correct: Order = 2 + 1 = 3, not 1+1 = 2. The exponent of NO is 2 and of O₂ is 1.
blocks.reason: Printing/calculation error. This reaction IS third order (2+1=3) and is listed in the third-order section, so the book contradicts itself.

blocks.head: Fractional Order Reaction
blocks.body: A reaction in which the sum of exponents of the rate equation is a fraction.
blocks.eq:
Rate = k[CHCl₃][Cl₂]^(1/2);   n = 1 + 0.5 = 1.5
Rate = k[A]^1.5
Rate = k[A][B]^(1/2)

Example: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl
Rate = k[CH₄][Cl₂]^(1/2);   order = 1.5
items: Reactions involving free radicals frequently exhibit fractional orders.
Sum of exponents is not a whole number.

blocks.head: General Formula for Units of k
blocks.body: The units of k depend on the overall order of the reaction.
blocks.eq:
kₙ = (mol dm⁻³)^(1–n) × s⁻¹

n = 0 (zero):    k = mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
n = 1 (first):   k = s⁻¹
n = 2 (second):  k = dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
n = 3 (third):   k = dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹

blocks.head: Worked Derivation — Units of k for 3rd Order Reaction
blocks.eq:
k = Rate / [A]³
  = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) / (mol dm⁻³)³
  = mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ / mol³ dm⁻⁹
  = mol^(1–3) × dm^(–3+9) × s⁻¹
  = mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹
  = dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹

items.q: For rate = k[NO]²[NH₃]⁰ and rate = k[BrO₃⁻][Br⁻][H⁺]²: find overall order and order w.r.t. each reactant.
items.ans:
Expression 1: rate = k[NO]²[NH₃]⁰
Overall order = 2+0 = 2
Order w.r.t. NO = 2; w.r.t. NH₃ = 0

Expression 2: rate = k[BrO₃⁻][Br⁻][H⁺]²
Overall order = 1+1+2 = 4
Order w.r.t. BrO₃⁻ = 1; Br⁻ = 1; H⁺ = 2

blocks.t: Sections 7.5 (Determination of Rate Constant, pp.154–155) and 7.6 (Reaction Mechanism, pp.156–158) are DELETED from the Smart Syllabus. Do NOT study for the board exam.

opts: Remains the same as the reaction proceeds
May decrease or increase as the reaction proceeds
mcqs.exp: As reaction proceeds, reactants are consumed → concentration falls → fewer effective collisions → rate decreases.

mcqs.q: Increasing the temperature of a chemical reaction increases the rate of a reaction because:
opts: Both the collision frequency and collision energies of reactant molecules increase
Collision frequency of reactant molecules increases only
mcqs.exp: Higher temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy (more energetic collisions) AND increases collision frequency. Both factors increase rate.

mcqs.q: Consider two reactions with different activation energies at the same temperature. The reaction with the lower activation energy will have:
opts: A rate constant that depends on the enthalpy change
mcqs.exp: Lower Ea → more molecules have E ≥ Ea → more effective collisions per second → larger rate constant k.

mcqs.q: The order of a chemical reaction that is independent of concentration is:
mcqs.exp: Zero order: Rate = k[A]⁰ = k. Concentration has no effect on rate; rate equals the rate constant.

mcqs.q: On a Boltzmann distribution curve, the area under the curve represents:
opts: Total number of molecules in the sample
Average kinetic energy of the molecules
mcqs.exp: The total area under the Boltzmann distribution curve represents the total number of molecules in the sample.

mcqs.q: On a Boltzmann distribution curve, the activation energy (Ea) is represented by:
opts: The area under the entire curve
A vertical line drawn at a specific kinetic energy value
The difference between the peak and the X-axis
mcqs.exp: Ea is marked as a vertical line at a specific energy value on the x-axis. Only molecules to the right of this line have E ≥ Ea.

mcqs.q: How does the presence of a catalyst affect the rate of a chemical reaction?
opts: It always decreases the rate of the reaction
It always increases the rate of the reaction
It increases the rate of the forward and decreases the rate of the reverse reaction
It increases the rate of both the forward and reverse reactions
mcqs.exp: A catalyst lowers Ea for both forward and reverse reactions equally, so rates of both increase. Equilibrium position is unchanged.

mcqs.q: On an energy profile diagram, the presence of a catalyst is represented by:
opts: A higher peak representing the activation energy
A lower peak representing the activation energy
A change in the energy level of the reactants or products
A shift in the equilibrium position
mcqs.exp: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower Ea, shown as a lower peak on the energy profile diagram.

mcqs.q: The units of the rate constant (k) for a reaction depend on the:
opts: Stoichiometry of the balanced chemical equation
mcqs.exp: Formula kₙ = (mol dm⁻³)^(1-n) s⁻¹ shows units depend on n (order). Order 0: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹; order 1: s⁻¹; order 2: dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

mcqs.q: For reaction 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g) with Rate = k[NO]²[O₂], the overall order is:
mcqs.exp: Overall order = sum of exponents = 2 (for NO) + 1 (for O₂) = 3.

opts: Catalyst and reactants are in different phases
Catalyst and reactants are in the same phase
mcqs.exp: Homogeneous catalysis: catalyst and reactants are in the same physical phase, forming a homogeneous mixture.

mcqs.q: The unit of rate constant k for a second order reaction is:
mcqs.exp: For n=2: k = (mol dm⁻³)^(1-2) s⁻¹ = mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹ = dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

mcqs.q: Rate = k[A]³. If [A] is doubled, the new rate becomes:
mcqs.exp: Third order: rate ∝ [A]³. New rate = k(2[A])³ = 8k[A]³ → rate increases 8 times.

sqs.q: What do you understand by the rate of a reaction?
sqs.a:
Definition: Rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product divided by the time taken for that change.

Rate = ΔC/Δt = –Δ[Reactant]/Δt = +Δ[Product]/Δt

Units: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ for fast reactions; mol dm⁻³ min⁻¹ for slow reactions.

Note: Rate decreases with time as reactant concentration falls. Negative sign = reactant consumed; positive sign = product formed.

sqs.q: Give the difference between enthalpy change of reaction and energy of activation of reaction.
sqs.a:
Enthalpy Change (ΔH):

  • Difference in energy between reactants and products.
  • Can be positive (endothermic) or negative (exothermic).
  • Tells us whether heat is released or absorbed overall.

Activation Energy (Ea):

  • Minimum energy required for effective collision between reacting species.
  • Always positive — energy must always be supplied to start a reaction.
  • Determines the rate — higher Ea = slower reaction.

Key Difference: ΔH = overall energy change of reaction; Ea = energy barrier that must be overcome to start the reaction. They are independent of each other.

sqs.q: Why does the instantaneous rate change during a reaction?
sqs.a:
Reason: Rate ∝ concentration. As reaction proceeds:

  • Reactants are consumed → reactant concentration decreases.
  • Fewer reactant particles per unit volume → fewer chances of collision.
  • Fewer effective collisions per second → instantaneous rate decreases with time.

Conclusion: Instantaneous rate is highest at the start (maximum concentration) and continuously falls as reactants are used up.

sqs.q: Briefly summarize the effects of temperature and surface area on the rates of reactions.
sqs.a:
Effect of Temperature:

  • Higher temperature → molecules gain more kinetic energy.
  • More molecules attain energy ≥ Ea (shaded area on Boltzmann curve increases).
  • More effective collisions per second → rate increases.
  • Rate doubles or triples for every 10°C rise in temperature.

Effect of Surface Area:

  • Rate ∝ surface area (binding sites exposed).
  • Greater surface area = more exposed particles = more chance of collision.
  • Powdered solids react faster than large lumps (e.g. CaCO₃ powder vs lumps with HCl).

sqs.q: Why does wood burn more rapidly in pure oxygen than in air?
sqs.a:
Reason — Effect of Concentration:

  • Air contains only about 21% oxygen.
  • Pure oxygen has a much higher concentration of O₂ molecules per unit volume.
  • Higher concentration → more O₂ molecules → more frequent and effective collisions with wood.
  • More effective collisions per second → combustion proceeds much faster.

Conclusion: The higher concentration of O₂ in pure oxygen increases collision frequency → rate of combustion increases.

sqs.q: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of a chemical reaction. Illustrate it.
sqs.a:
Definition: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy (Ea).

How it works:

  • Without catalyst: reactants must overcome a high Ea barrier → slow reaction.
  • With catalyst: molecules are brought into correct orientation and a new lower-Ea pathway is available.
  • More molecules now have energy ≥ new (lower) Ea → more effective collisions → faster rate.
  • Products have the same energy with or without catalyst — only Ea is lowered.

Energy profile illustration:

Energy | | /\ ← uncatalyzed (high Ea) | / \ /\ ← catalyzed (low Ea) |/ \ / \ R * P |___________________→ Reaction progress

sqs.q: How does the activation energy profile of an uncatalyzed reaction compare with that of the catalyzed reaction?
sqs.a:
Uncatalyzed reaction:

  • Reactants must go over a high energy barrier (large Ea).
  • Only few molecules have E ≥ large Ea → slow rate.
  • Energy profile shows a tall peak between reactants and products.

Catalyzed reaction:

  • Catalyst provides a new alternative pathway with a lower Ea.
  • More molecules now have E ≥ smaller Ea → faster rate.
  • Energy profile shows a shorter (lower) peak on the same diagram.

Key points for both:

  • Energy of reactants and products remains the same — ΔH is unchanged.
  • Catalyst lowers Ea for both forward AND reverse reactions equally.
  • Equilibrium position is not changed, only the rate at which equilibrium is reached.

sqs.q: Calculate the reaction rate if [A] = 0.5 M, [B] = 0.2 M and rate constant k = 4.0 M⁻² s⁻¹. Given rate law: Rate = k[A][B]².
sqs.a:
Given:

  • [A] = 0.5 mol dm⁻³
  • [B] = 0.2 mol dm⁻³
  • k = 4.0 dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹
  • Rate = k[A][B]²

Solution:

Rate = k[A][B]² = 4.0 × (0.5) × (0.2)² = 4.0 × 0.5 × 0.04 = 4.0 × 0.02 = 0.08 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

Answer: Rate = 0.08 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

sqs.q: Differentiate between homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysis with one example each.
sqs.a:
Homogeneous Catalysis:

  • Catalyst and reactants are in the SAME physical phase.
  • Forms a homogeneous mixture.
  • Example: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g); catalyst: NO(g) — all gases.

Heterogeneous Catalysis:

  • Catalyst and reactants are in DIFFERENT phases.
  • Does NOT form a homogeneous mixture.
  • Example: C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g); catalyst: Ni(s) — solid catalyst, gaseous reactants.

sqs.q: Explain the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve and how it explains the effect of temperature on rate of reaction.
sqs.a:
Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution Curve: A graph between number of molecules (y-axis) and kinetic energy (x-axis) at a specific temperature. At any given temperature:

  • Few molecules have very low energy.
  • Few molecules have very high energy.
  • Most molecules have moderate/average energy.
  • Shaded area (E ≥ Ea) = molecules capable of effective collision.

Effect of Temperature Rise (T₁ → T₂):

  • Curve flattens and shifts to the right.
  • Shaded area approximately doubles for every 10°C rise.
  • More molecules have E ≥ Ea → more effective collisions → rate doubles or triples.

lqs.title: Q6(b) — Rate Law, Order of Reaction and Units of Rate Constant
lqs.q: What is rate law? Explain different orders of reaction (zero, first, second, third, fractional) with examples. Also give the units of rate constant for each order.

parts.label: RATE LAW AND RATE CONSTANT
points: Rate law: equation that relates rate of reaction to concentrations of reactants raised to various powers: Rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ.
k = rate constant (specific rate constant) — the rate of reaction when all reactant concentrations are unity (1 mol dm⁻³).
Exponents x and y are determined experimentally — NOT from stoichiometric coefficients.
Overall order = x + y (sum of all exponents in rate equation).
k remains constant at a fixed temperature but changes with temperature.
General unit formula: kₙ = (mol dm⁻³)^(1−n) s⁻¹ where n = order.

parts.label: ZERO ORDER
points: Rate = k[A]⁰ = k. Rate is independent of concentration.
Doubling or halving concentration has NO effect on rate.
Example: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl (sunlight). Photochemical reactions are usually zero order.
Unit of k: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

parts.label: FIRST ORDER
points: Rate = k[A]¹. Rate depends on concentration of one reactant (sum of exponents = 1).
Doubling concentration doubles the rate.
Example: N₂O₅ → 2NO₂ + ½O₂; Rate = k[N₂O₅]¹. Nuclear decay is always first order.
Unit of k: s⁻¹.

parts.label: SECOND ORDER
points: Rate = k[A]² or k[A][B]. Sum of exponents = 2.
Example: NO + O₃ → NO₂ + O₂; Rate = k[NO][O₃]; order = 1+1 = 2.
Doubling one reactant in Rate = k[A]²: rate becomes 4× (quadruples).
Unit of k: dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

parts.label: THIRD AND FRACTIONAL ORDER
points: Third order: sum of exponents = 3. Rate = k[A]³, k[A]²[B], or k[A][B][C].
Example: 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂; Rate = k[NO]²[O₂]¹; order = 2+1 = 3. Unit of k: dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹.
Fractional order: sum of exponents is a fraction. Example: CHCl₃ + Cl₂ → CCl₄ + HCl; Rate = k[CHCl₃][Cl₂]^(1/2); order = 1.5.
Fractional orders are common in free radical reactions.

lqs.title: Q6(b) Alt — Factors Affecting Rate of Reaction
lqs.q: Describe the factors that affect the rate of a chemical reaction. Explain temperature using the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve and catalyst using an energy profile diagram.

parts.label: CONCENTRATION
points: Rate ∝ concentration (law of mass action).
More concentration → more particles per unit volume → more chances of collision.
Effective collisions increase → rate increases.
Example: Higher CO₂ concentration → higher rate of photosynthesis.
For gases: higher pressure = higher concentration → higher rate.

parts.label: TEMPERATURE AND MAXWELL-BOLTZMANN CURVE
points: Rate doubles or triples for every 10°C rise in temperature.
Maxwell-Boltzmann curve: graph of number of molecules (y-axis) vs kinetic energy (x-axis).
At any temperature: few molecules have very low or very high energy; most have moderate energy.
Shaded area (E ≥ Ea) = molecules capable of effective collision.
When temperature rises: curve flattens and shifts right; shaded area doubles → more effective collisions → rate doubles.

parts.label: SURFACE AREA
points: Rate ∝ surface area (number of binding sites).
Greater surface area = more exposed particles = more chance of collision.
Powdered solids react faster than large lumps.

parts.label: CATALYST AND ENERGY PROFILE
points: Catalyst: substance that alters rate but remains chemically unchanged at the end.
Catalyst provides alternative reaction pathway with lower Ea.
More molecules have energy ≥ new lower Ea → more effective collisions → higher rate.
Energy profile: catalyzed reaction has lower peak (lower Ea); products at same energy level.
Homogeneous catalysis: catalyst and reactants in same phase (e.g. NO(g) in Contact process).
Heterogeneous catalysis: catalyst and reactants in different phases (e.g. Ni(s) in hydrogenation).

quiz.q: Reaction kinetics is the study of:
quiz.exp: Reaction kinetics deals with rates of reactions, factors affecting rates, and reaction mechanisms.

quiz.q: For a slow reaction, the unit of rate of reaction is:
quiz.exp: For slow reactions, time is measured in minutes so unit = mol dm⁻³ min⁻¹. Fast reactions use s⁻¹.

quiz.q: For reaction A → B, the rate expression with respect to product is:
quiz.exp: Product concentration increases with time → positive sign: Rate = +Δ[B]/Δt.

quiz.q: According to collision theory, effective collisions require:
opts: Both proper orientation and energy ≥ Ea
quiz.exp: Both conditions must be met: particles must be properly oriented AND have energy ≥ activation energy (Ea).

quiz.q: The rate of reaction is measured graphically by finding:
opts: Slope of the tangent to the concentration–time curve
Gradient of the straight line portion only
quiz.exp: Instantaneous rate = slope (gradient) of tangent drawn at a specific point on the concentration–time curve.

quiz.q: Spectrophotometry measures rate by tracking changes in:
quiz.exp: Spectrophotometry measures rate by monitoring the amount of UV, visible, or IR radiation absorbed by a reactant or product.

quiz.q: For the reaction N₂O₅ → 2NO₂ + ½O₂, Rate = k[N₂O₅]¹. The reaction is:
quiz.exp: The exponent of N₂O₅ is 1 → first order reaction.

quiz.q: Which of the following is always a first order reaction?
quiz.exp: Nuclear (radioactive) decay is always first order because rate depends only on the amount of radioactive isotope present.

quiz.q: Rate = k[A]²[B]. What is the order with respect to A?
quiz.exp: The exponent of [A] is 2, so the reaction is second order with respect to A.

quiz.q: The unit of k for a zero order reaction is:
quiz.exp: n=0: k = (mol dm⁻³)^(1-0) s⁻¹ = mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

quiz.q: Increasing concentration increases rate because:
quiz.exp: More particles per unit volume → more frequent collisions → more effective collisions → higher rate.

quiz.q: In the Boltzmann distribution curve, the shaded area represents:
opts: Molecules with energy less than Ea
Molecules with energy equal to or greater than Ea
quiz.exp: Shaded area = molecules with E ≥ Ea = molecules capable of effective (productive) collision.

quiz.q: When temperature rises, the Boltzmann distribution curve:
quiz.exp: At higher temperature, more molecules have higher energy → curve flattens (lower peak) and shifts to the right.

quiz.q: The hydrogenation C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆ with Ni catalyst is:
quiz.exp: Ni is solid; reactants are gases → different phases → heterogeneous catalysis.

quiz.q: For reaction CHCl₃ + Cl₂ → CCl₄ + HCl, Rate = k[CHCl₃][Cl₂]^(1/2). The order is:
quiz.exp: Order = 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 — this is a fractional order reaction common in free radical processes.

quiz.q: A catalyst increases reaction rate by:
opts: Providing an alternative pathway with lower Ea
quiz.exp: Catalyst lowers Ea by providing an alternative reaction pathway, so more molecules can react per second.

quiz.q: For rate = k[A][B]², overall order is 3. If [B] is doubled, the rate becomes:
quiz.exp: Rate ∝ [B]². Doubling [B] → rate = k[A](2[B])² = 4k[A][B]² → rate becomes 4 times.

quiz.q: The specific rate constant k equals the rate of reaction when:
opts: Half the reactant has been consumed
quiz.exp: When [A]=[B]=1 mol dm⁻³, Rate = k×1ˣ×1ʸ = k. So k = rate at unit concentrations.

quiz.q: Which method is used to measure rate of a reaction involving formation of ions?
quiz.exp: Formation of ions changes electrical conductivity of solution. Rate ∝ conductivity for ion-forming reactions.

quiz.q: In the Contact process 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃, catalyst NO(g) represents:
quiz.exp: NO gas catalyst with SO₂ and O₂ gas reactants — all in the same (gas) phase → homogeneous catalysis.
